title: Leading the Project Team
sequence: Executing: Lead the Team runs from team formation through to release of the team; the project manager adapts the style as the team and situation change.

header.html: People domain (33%) · Task 3 Lead the project team — establish expectations at the team level · empower the team · solve problems · represent the voice of the team · support the team's varied experiences, skills and perspectives · determine an appropriate leadership style · establish clear roles and responsibilities within the team

[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (ECO wording, common exam practice, mock-exam style).

toc.title: Leading the Project Team: the Seven Enablers
Establish Expectations at the Team Level
Represent the Voice of the Team
Support Varied Experiences, Skills and Perspectives
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Lead the Team Applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to manage and lead the team by improving competencies, team member interactions and the team environment to raise performance; includes tracking performance, giving feedback, resolving and escalating issues and managing team changes
Management activities Focus on the means of meeting objectives: effective processes, planning, coordinating, measuring, monitoring
Leadership activities Focus on people: influencing, motivating, listening, enabling
Leadership The knowledge, skills and behaviors to guide, motivate and direct a team to achieve business goals (negotiation, resilience, communication, problem-solving, critical thinking, interpersonal skills). Useful to all members, whether authority is centralized or shared
Servant leadership Leading by understanding and addressing the needs and development of team members to enable the highest team performance, in service of the project's objectives
Centralized vs distributed management and leadership Centralized: authority and decisions held by a few senior leaders, accountability usually with one person (the PM). Distributed: decision-making and authority spread among individuals and teams; the team may self-organize and the facilitator role may rotate
Team development Improving the team's skills, interactions and environment through training, team building, coaching, colocation and assessment
Tuckman ladder Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
Team charter The team's values, communication guidelines, decision-making, conflict resolution, meeting guidelines and agreements (Topic 19)
Team performance assessment Formal or informal evaluation of team effectiveness: skills and competency improvements, lower turnover, higher cohesiveness
Empowerment Giving the team authority and autonomy over how it works, within defined boundaries
Emotional intelligence (EI) The ability to identify, assess and manage one's own and others' emotions, and group emotions
Organizational cultural intelligence The capability to perform effectively in culturally diverse, complex situations without careless stereotyping

2Leading the Project Team: the Seven Enablers

Process view (PMBOK 8): inputs include the resource management plan, issue log, lessons learned register, schedule, resource calendars, team charter, work performance reports, team assignments and team performance assessments. Tools include colocation, virtual teams, communication technology, interpersonal and team skills (conflict management, influencing, motivation, negotiation, team building, decision-making, critical thinking, coaching and mentoring, training, problem-solving, Six Thinking Hats, retrospectives, recognition and rewards, individual and team assessments), SWOT analysis, meetings, emotional intelligence, organizational cultural intelligence, leadership styles (distributed, centralized, servant), Tuckman ladder, PMIS and virtual collaboration tools. Outputs: team performance assessments, change requests, and updates to plans, issue log, lessons learned, team charter and assignments.

3Establish Expectations at the Team Level

  • Vision and objectives: communicate them throughout and use them when the team decides and solves problems. A good vision is clear, concise and actionable: it summarizes the project in a powerful phrase, describes the best achievable outcome, creates a common picture and inspires. Built with the team and key stakeholders it answers: what is the purpose, what defines success, how will the future be better, and how will we know we are drifting? (Topic 11)
  • Team charter and working agreements: co-created values, communication norms, decision-making, conflict resolution, meeting rules; revisit them when new members join and when the context changes; everyone shares responsibility for following them (Topic 19).
  • Ground rules and norms: agreed behavior, with a way to handle violations (Topic 26).
  • Performance and quality expectations: definition of done, acceptance criteria, quality standards, reporting expectations.
  • Kickoff: a deliberate start (purpose, roles, how decisions are made, how we communicate).
  • Guidance and growth: direction for the whole team; goals for improvement; support for individuals' development goals.

4Determine an Appropriate Leadership Style

Factors to weigh: team maturity and stage; individual competence and willingness; task complexity, urgency and risk; organizational culture and governance (centralized or distributed); development approach; team location; the project's newness to the organization (new work calls for more oversight and a more direct style; experienced teams are more self-managing).

Situation Style emphasis
Newly formed team, unclear roles Directing and structuring: vision, roles, expectations, ground rules
Conflict over approach Coaching and facilitating: surface issues, reinforce agreements
Maturing team Supporting and delegating
High-performing, experienced team Servant leadership and empowerment: remove impediments, delegate, protect
Crisis, safety, compliance Directive for the moment, then return to the normal style and review
Low trust or cross-organization team More up-front work to build a "one team" mindset
Matrix environment, little authority Influence: be persuasive, articulate positions clearly, listen actively, consider perspectives, gather information, keep mutual trust

Common style vocabulary [Beyond PMBOK 8]: directive (autocratic), consultative, participative (democratic), delegating (laissez-faire), coaching, servant, transformational (inspires change), transactional (rewards for performance). PMBOK 8 pairs: Theory X (hands-on, top-down) vs Theory Y (coaching, creativity) vs Theory Z (meaning and well-being); centralized vs distributed leadership; servant leadership as the model for self-managing teams.

Situational leadership (PMBOK 8 names it; the four-style model is Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice): choose the style from the person's competence and commitment for that task, and change it as they grow.

Follower's level for the task Style
Low competence, high commitment (an eager beginner) Directing: tell, show and check closely
Some competence, commitment dropping (a discouraged learner) Coaching: explain, ask questions, encourage
High competence, variable confidence Supporting: listen, praise, share the decision
High competence and high commitment Delegating: agree the outcome and leave the how to them

Main risk when a style is overused [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]:

Style Strength Risk when overused
Servant Serves the team and clears the way Decisions drift when the team needs a firm call
Transactional Clear rewards and penalties for results People do only what is rewarded; initiative fades
Transformational Inspires commitment to change and to the vision Constant stretch exhausts people and routine controls slip
Laissez-faire Maximum autonomy for a mature team Without direction, goals blur and disputes fester
Directive (autocratic) Speed and clarity in a crisis Resentment, passivity, little ownership
Participative (democratic) Buy-in and better decisions Slow decisions and blurred accountability

5Empower the Team

  • Delegate decisions about how work is done and about details of deliverables, within clear boundaries (decision rights, guardrails, escalation points). Empowered members perform better and are more satisfied than micromanaged ones.
  • Create the conditions: trust, clarity of purpose, skills, information, safety to speak and to fail, authority that matches responsibility.
  • Motivate through autonomy, mastery and purpose (section 8): flexible ways of working, learning, and a line of sight to the vision.
  • Stay available: coach, remove barriers, protect the team from outside interference; do not abdicate.
  • Escalate decisions beyond the team's authority with analysis and recommendation.
  • Agile and distributed teams self-organize; the PM acts as servant leader and facilitator rather than task director. The PM remains accountable for the environment and for escalation.

Two signals to read correctly [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]:

Situation Best response
Delivery metrics look healthy (steady velocity, milestones met), but morale has dropped and the team has stopped proposing ideas Metrics can hide disengagement. Meet the team to understand what changed and what support they need before choosing recognition, a new format or a higher target
A mature team that backs its decisions with evidence still has its daily tasks assigned by the project manager Let the team decide how to distribute daily work within agreed goals and boundaries. Handing task assignment to a few senior members only builds a new hierarchy

6Solve Problems

Structured problem-solving (PMBOK 8): define the problem; identify the root cause; generate possible solutions; choose the best; implement it; verify effectiveness.

Tool Use
Critical thinking Question assumptions, spot bias and faulty logic, gather unbiased information, analyze evidence; find root causes
Root cause and cause-and-effect analysis Trace problems to their underlying causes (Topic 18)
Six Thinking Hats A group discussion technique using six colored "hats" for ways of thinking: blue (facilitates, big picture), white (facts), red (feelings), black (cautions and negatives), plus yellow (positives) and green (creative ideas)
Decision-making Voting, multicriteria analysis, diverge then converge to limit groupthink (Topic 14)
Retrospectives Regular workshops to improve process and product with actionable items

Leader behaviors: facilitate rather than solve everything yourself; involve the people closest to the work; decide quickly when the team cannot; escalate beyond authority with alternatives ("do not bring me problems, bring me solutions"); close the loop and verify the fix.

7Represent the Voice of the Team

  • Speak for the team to the sponsor, governance and stakeholders: capacity limits, impediments, risks, needs and achievements. When the team asks you to represent it (for example against unplanned mid-iteration requests), do so.
  • Protect the team: route new requests through the backlog or change process, show trade-offs and capacity data, and negotiate priorities.
  • Bring insight upward and decisions downward transparently; share credit.
  • Do not speak for the team without their input, and do not filter their concerns.
  • Remove impediments the team cannot (Topic 30).

8Support Varied Experiences, Skills and Perspectives

  • Inclusion and safety: create a safe, respectful, nonjudgmental environment; welcome disagreement ("positive discourse": dialogue, not win-lose debate); show courage by inviting and accepting challenge.
  • Adapt to people: different styles need different forms of participation (for example written or asynchronous input for members who are quiet in meetings but strong in writing). Adapt the process rather than force individuals to change.
  • Mix seniority and expertise to create coaching and mentoring (coaching: asking questions to help a person find a solution to a specific problem; mentoring: long-term guidance by sharing experience). Act on offers of mentoring.
  • Cultural intelligence: recognize that people from different cultures think and express themselves differently, without stereotyping; adjust communication and recognition to culture.
  • Transparency about bias (the PM's own and the team's) builds openness and trust.
  • Skill matrix and assessments: see strengths and gaps; plan training (Topic 19); use individual and team assessments (attitudinal surveys, structured interviews, focus groups) to understand preferences and strengths.
  • Emotional intelligence: four areas: self-awareness (realistic self-assessment), self-management (think before acting), social awareness (empathy, reading cues), social skills (rapport, building teams, finding common ground). EI is the basis of all forms of leadership; emotionally competent teams are more effective with less turnover.
  • Well-being: watch workload and signs of burnout; support flexible schedules and stress management (Topic 19).

9Establish Clear Roles and Responsibilities

  • Roles (functions), responsibilities (duties), authority (right to decide, approve and apply resources) and competence (skill and capacity). Authority should match responsibility.
  • Use the responsibility assignment matrix / RACI (one accountable owner per activity), position descriptions and role-responsibility-authority forms (Topic 19).
  • Fill competence gaps through training, coaching, mentoring or reassignment.
  • Agile roles: product owner (value and backlog), development team members (build, self-organize), facilitator or coach; titles vary, the functions matter.
  • Vendors and partners: clarify who directs whose people and the reporting lines (Topic 22); define handoffs and confirmation points.
  • Revisit when people join, leave or change roles.

10Motivation and Recognition

Theory Core idea Cue in a scenario
Maslow (PMBOK 8 mentions it; the five levels are Beyond PMBOK 8) Needs run from physiological and safety through belonging and esteem to self-actualization; a satisfied need stops motivating A member whose basic needs are met now asks for status and a chance to grow
Herzberg Hygiene factors (policy, pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, recognition, growth) create satisfaction A raise ends the complaints but not the boredom
McClelland Needs for achievement, power (influence) and affiliation One member volunteers for stretch goals and wants feedback; another keeps building relationships
McGregor X, Y and Z X: people avoid work unless watched; Y: people seek responsibility and direct themselves; Z (Ouchi): long-term commitment and well-being A manager checks every task because "people slack off otherwise" (X)
Pink Intrinsic drivers: autonomy, mastery, purpose Once pay is fair, more money adds little
Vroom (expectancy) Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice Motivation is high when people believe effort leads to performance, performance leads to a reward, and the reward is valued A bonus exists, but staff doubt that extra effort will change the rating that triggers it
  • Understand what motivates each person and keep them committed; empower the team in decisions and encourage independent work.
  • Recognition and rewards: the plan starts in Plan Resource Management; cultural differences change what is meaningful; money is tangible but intangible rewards can be as or more effective; most members are motivated by growth, accomplishment, appreciation and applying their skills. Recognize throughout the project, not only at the end; celebrate successes and quick wins.
  • Team building: from a five-minute agenda item to an off-site event; valuable for remote teams; essential early, but a continuous process as the environment changes.
  • Training: formal or informal; scheduled or unplanned; costs may sit in the project budget or be supported by the organization.

11High-Performing Teams and Team Development

Characteristics (PMBOK 8): open communication, shared understanding, shared ownership, trust, collaboration, adaptability, resilience, empowerment and autonomy, recognition.

Leader role-modeling (PMBOK 8 §2.6.3):

Behavior What it looks like
Transparency Open about how you think and decide, including your biases
Integrity Honest about risks and assumptions; deliver bad news early; accurate status; disclose conflicts of interest
Respect For each person's thinking, skills and expertise
Positive discourse Dialogue to resolve differences, not debate to win
Support Solve problems with the team, remove impediments, show empathy and listen
Courage Suggest new approaches and disagree with authority respectfully
Celebrate success Recognize progress, innovation and learning

Team performance assessment indicators: improved skills and competencies, lower turnover, greater cohesion and information sharing. Use the findings to choose training, coaching or other changes.

Virtual teams and colocation (Topic 19): use technology and relationship time to build trust; hold at least one face-to-face meeting where possible.

12Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Leadership model Centralized; project manager directs and coordinates Distributed and servant leadership; team self-organizes; facilitator or coach Centralized for the envelope; distributed inside iterations
Roles Defined by the RAM, functional or matrix roles Product owner, team, facilitator; cross-functional Both
Team makeup Functional specialists assigned from managers Dedicated, cross-functional, about 3 to 9 members Mix
Decision-making Escalation and approval chains Team decides how; product owner decides priority Both
Improvement Lessons learned at gates Retrospective every iteration Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 Psychological safety as the foundation for candid retrospectives

13Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor to the development approach, team maturity and experience, cross-organization teams, culture and bias, industry context, governance structure (centralized or distributed), sustainability, virtual teams and well-being (Topic 19).
  • Interactions: leadership affects every domain: stakeholder engagement (trust and influence), communication, risk (psychological safety to raise risks), quality (ownership), schedule and cost (capacity and morale).
  • Check results (Table 2-10): all members know the vision; the team owns deliverables and outcomes; members trust and collaborate; the team adapts and is resilient; members feel empowered and recognized while delivering results.

14Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Match style to the stage and situation. New teams need structure and direction; storming teams need facilitation; mature teams need delegation; crises may need a directive style briefly.
  2. Do not impose a decision to end a storming debate; facilitate and reinforce the team's agreements.
  3. Empower within boundaries: define decision rights; do not micromanage, and do not abdicate.
  4. Represent the team's voice and protect its capacity when it asks you to.
  5. Adapt the process to people (written input, flexible participation), do not force people to change their nature.
  6. Authority must match responsibility; one accountable owner per activity; clarify vendor and team reporting lines.
  7. Co-create and revisit the team charter, especially when new members join.
  8. Recognize early and often, in ways that fit the culture; do not wait for project end.
  9. Motivate with growth, autonomy and purpose once pay is fair; money alone does not solve disengagement.
  10. Facilitate problem-solving; let the people with expertise decide within their authority; escalate with options when beyond it.
  11. Coach by asking questions; mentor over time; act on mentoring offers.
  12. Watch for burnout and disengagement; adjust workload and support well-being.
  13. Servant leadership is the default for self-managing teams (understand and meet team needs, remove barriers), but it does not mean lack of accountability.
  14. Model the behaviors you want: transparency, integrity, respect, positive discourse, support, courage.
  15. Use influence, not authority, in matrix environments.
  16. Do not speak for the team without their input.
  17. Healthy metrics can hide a disengaged team; talk to the people first. When a team is mature, widen its decision rights within goals instead of tightening task control.

15Exam Q&A

15.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Courteous in the first sprints, the members of a new agile team now openly challenge the plan, each other's methods and the project manager's authority. Which leadership emphasis fits best?

  • ADelegating, by stepping back until the team has sorted out its differences
  • BDirecting, by deciding every contested point and ending the debate quickly
  • CCoaching and facilitating, surfacing issues and reinforcing the team's agreements
  • DSupporting, by praising the team and leaving the disagreements unaddressed
Show the answer

Answer: C. Open challenge and conflict mark the storming stage, which calls for coaching and facilitation that surface the issues and reinforce the team's own agreements. Imposing decisions suppresses ideas, stepping back leaves the team unsupported, and praise alone ignores the conflict.

S2An experienced agile team still sends every minor decision to the project manager, who has become a bottleneck. What should the project manager do?

  • ATake the decisions faster by checking messages several times a day
  • BDefine decision rights, delegate within them, and coach the team to decide
  • CAdd a deputy who approves the team's decisions whenever the project manager is busy
  • DAsk the sponsor to rule on the team's decisions to speed up approvals
Show the answer

Answer: B. Empowerment means clear boundaries and delegation, with coaching until the team is comfortable, so the experienced team decides how it works. Faster approvals, another approval layer or sponsor rulings keep the decisions outside the team.

S3As a two-year project nears its end, morale dips because team members worry about their next assignments. What should the project manager do?

  • ASay nothing about assignments until the closing report has been submitted
  • BReplace the most anxious members now to protect the team's morale
  • CRecognize contributions and help members plan their transitions
  • DKeep the whole team fully assigned until the very last day of the project
Show the answer

Answer: C. In the adjourning stage, leaders recognize achievements, help people prepare for their next roles and release resources in an orderly way. Keeping everyone assigned to the end, staying silent on assignments or replacing anxious members ignores the transition.

S4The sponsor asks whether the scrum team agrees with a new, earlier release date, and the project manager is tempted to answer yes on the team's behalf. What is the better approach?

  • AAnswer yes now, since the project manager is accountable for the team's commitments
  • BAsk the sponsor to put the question to the team members one by one
  • CAnswer no without discussion, because earlier deadlines always add risk
  • DConsult the team first, then give the sponsor its view together with capacity data
Show the answer

Answer: D. Representing the voice of the team means speaking with its input, not for it, and bringing capacity data and concerns to the sponsor. Answering for the team in either direction, or passing the question to the sponsor to ask individually, skips that consultation.

S5A design discussion in backlog refinement keeps stalling because people mix facts, feelings and objections in the same breath. Which technique offers structured parallel thinking?

  • AA SWOT analysis, in which the group lists the strengths and weaknesses of the design
  • BMajority voting, in which each member votes before any discussion takes place
  • CA Pareto chart, in which the group ranks the objections by frequency
  • DSix Thinking Hats, with the group using one way of thinking at a time
Show the answer

Answer: D. Six Thinking Hats separates ways of thinking (facts, feelings, cautions, positives, creativity and process) so that the group handles one at a time. Voting, SWOT and Pareto organize decisions, options or frequencies but do not separate modes of thinking.

S6After a sharp email from a stakeholder, the project manager pauses to cool down before replying. Which area of emotional intelligence is being used?

  • ASelf-management, which means thinking before acting
  • BSocial skills, which means building rapport with the stakeholder
  • CSocial awareness, which means reading the emotions of the whole group
  • DSelf-awareness, which means recognizing the stakeholder's feelings in the email
Show the answer

Answer: A. Self-management is the ability to regulate one's own reactions and think before acting. Self-awareness is realistic self-assessment, social awareness is empathy and reading cues, and social skills are rapport and team building.

S7A well-paid team has lost its enthusiasm, and the sponsor proposes a larger bonus pool. What is likely to add more motivation?

  • AA leaderboard that ranks the members by the number of tasks they complete
  • BA larger bonus, since money is the strongest long-term motivator for most people
  • CTighter supervision, so that effort is visible and underperformance is corrected
  • DGrowth opportunities, more autonomy and a clear line of sight to the project's purpose
Show the answer

Answer: D. Once pay is fair, most people are motivated by growth, accomplishment, appreciation and purpose, and intangible rewards can be as effective as money. A bigger bonus, tighter supervision or rankings do not address engagement.

S8At a team meeting, the project manager publicly praises everyone by name, and a member from a culture that values modesty looks uncomfortable. How should recognition be adapted?

  • ARecognize the member in a form that fits the culture, such as a private thank-you
  • BKeep the public praise, because every member should be treated in exactly the same way
  • CAsk the member to explain in front of the group why the praise is unwelcome
  • DStop recognizing anyone, since recognition always makes some people uncomfortable
Show the answer

Answer: A. Cultural differences change what recognition is meaningful, so the project manager adapts the form while continuing to recognize contributions. Withholding recognition, applying one rule to all or putting the member on the spot ignores the difference.

S9A team lead is accountable for the quality of a module but cannot reject substandard work from the other teams that feed it. What should the project manager do?

  • AMake the project manager accountable for the quality of every module
  • BGive the lead matching authority, such as acceptance rights, or change the accountability
  • CAsk the lead to report problems to the project manager at the end of each month
  • DLeave the arrangement, since accountability always carries some frustration with it
Show the answer

Answer: B. Authority should match responsibility, so the lead either gets the authority to accept or reject incoming work or the accountability is reassigned. Leaving the mismatch, delayed reporting or making the project manager accountable for everything does not fix it.

S10A self-managing team has missed its goals for three sprints, and the project manager, believing servant leadership means non-interference, has stayed silent. What was wrong?

  • AServant leadership still means accountability: helping the team inspect causes
  • BThe team should have asked the sponsor to assign a new project manager
  • CThe project manager should have taken over the team's decisions as a directive leader
  • DNothing, because a self-managing team must always solve its own problems alone
Show the answer

Answer: A. Servant leadership means meeting the team's needs and removing barriers, not abdicating accountability, so the project manager helps the team examine why goals are missed. Leaving the team alone, taking over or seeking a replacement all misread the role.

S11A junior member disagrees with a senior colleague in a meeting, and the senior says the team does not debate decisions made by experts. How should the project manager model positive discourse?

  • AAsk the junior member to raise any disagreement in writing after the meeting
  • BWelcome the challenge and steer the group to a dialogue about the evidence
  • CLet the two members argue it out until one of them concedes the point
  • DSupport the senior colleague, since experience should settle technical questions
Show the answer

Answer: B. Positive discourse means dialogue to resolve differences rather than debate to win, and leaders show courage by inviting and accepting challenge. Deferring to seniority, moving the disagreement out of the room or letting a win-lose argument continue undermines it.

S12After a year, the sponsor asks how the project manager knows the team has improved. Which indicators does a team performance assessment use?

  • AThe project's cost variance and the number of change requests approved
  • BThe number of meetings held and the hours logged by each member
  • CImproved skills and competencies, lower turnover and greater cohesion
  • DThe number of deliverables completed per month, regardless of their quality
Show the answer

Answer: C. A team performance assessment looks at improvements in skills and competencies, lower turnover and higher cohesion, then uses the findings to choose training or other changes. Meetings, cost variance and output counts measure activity or project performance rather than team effectiveness.

15.2 Recall Q&As

R1Management versus leadership activities in Lead the Team?

Show the answer

Management focuses on the means of meeting objectives (processes, planning, coordinating, measuring, monitoring); leadership focuses on people (influencing, motivating, listening, enabling).

R2Name the Tuckman stages.

Show the answer

Forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning; teams can get stuck, regress or skip stages.

R3What is servant leadership?

Show the answer

Leading by understanding and addressing team members' needs and development to enable the highest performance, in service of project objectives.

R4Centralized versus distributed management and leadership?

Show the answer

Centralized: decisions and authority with a few senior leaders and accountability with one person; distributed: authority spread among individuals and teams, possibly self-organizing.

R5Herzberg's hygiene versus motivational factors?

Show the answer

Hygiene factors (policies, salary, environment) prevent dissatisfaction but do not create satisfaction; motivational factors (achievement, growth, advancement) create satisfaction.

R6What are Pink's three intrinsic motivators?

Show the answer

Autonomy, mastery and purpose.

R7What are McClelland's three needs?

Show the answer

Achievement, power and affiliation.

R8Theory X, Y and Z?

Show the answer

X: people work for income, so a hands-on top-down style; Y: people are intrinsically motivated, so a coaching style; Z: self-realization and meaning (Maslow) or employee well-being and long-term commitment (Ouchi).

R9Coaching versus mentoring?

Show the answer

Coaching helps a person find their own solution to a specific problem by asking questions; mentoring is a long-term relationship of sharing knowledge and experience.

R10What does a team charter include?

Show the answer

Values, communication guidelines, decision-making criteria and processes, conflict resolution, meeting guidelines and team agreements.

R11List the characteristics of high-performing teams.

Show the answer

Open communication, shared understanding, shared ownership, trust, collaboration, adaptability, resilience, empowerment and autonomy, and recognition.

R12What are the four areas of emotional intelligence?

Show the answer

Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and social skills.

R13What are key influencing skills?

Show the answer

Being persuasive, articulating positions clearly, active listening, considering other perspectives, and gathering information while maintaining mutual trust.

R14What do team performance assessments look at?

Show the answer

Skills and competency improvements, staff turnover and team cohesiveness; they guide training, coaching or other changes.

16Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Lead the Team Improve competencies, interactions and environment; feedback, collaboration, conflict resolution, escalation
Seven enablers Expectations · empower · solve problems · voice of the team · varied perspectives · style · roles
Management vs leadership Means (processes, planning, measuring) vs people (influencing, motivating, listening, enabling)
Tuckman Forming (structure) → storming (coach, facilitate) → norming (support, delegate) → performing (empower) → adjourning (recognize, transition)
Servant leadership Meet team needs, remove barriers; default for self-managing teams
Centralized vs distributed Authority with a few vs spread across the team
Empowerment Delegate within clear boundaries; avoid micromanaging; escalate beyond authority
Problem-solving Define, root cause, options, choose, implement, verify; critical thinking; Six Thinking Hats
Voice of the team Represent capacity and needs; protect from unplanned demands
Varied perspectives Inclusion, safety, written input, mentoring, cultural intelligence
Roles RACI; one accountable; authority matches responsibility; vendor and agile roles
Motivation Herzberg (hygiene vs motivators), Pink (autonomy, mastery, purpose), McClelland (achievement, power, affiliation), McGregor (X, Y, Z)
Recognition Throughout the project; tailored to culture; intangible can beat money
